faq.q: How does the tool know if my number is seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds?
faq.a: It counts the digits. A value with up to 11 digits is read as seconds, up to 14 as milliseconds, up to 17 as microseconds, and longer as nanoseconds — so 1700000000 is seconds and 1700000000000 is milliseconds. The sign is ignored for counting, so negative (pre-1970) values are detected the same way. You can override the guess with the unit dropdown if your value is unusual.

faq.q: Why does the Date to Timestamp result use the time zone I pick instead of my computer's?
faq.a: Because the same wall-clock time means a different instant in each zone. The tool reads your date and time as if they were written on a clock in the zone you choose, works out that zone's exact offset for that specific date (including daylight saving) using the browser's time zone data, and then produces the epoch. That is why 2026-01-01 00:00 in Asia/Kolkata gives 1767205800, not whatever your own zone would give.

faq.q: What happens with a daylight-saving gap or an ambiguous time?
faq.a: On the spring-forward date some wall-clock times do not exist (the clock jumps, e.g. 02:30 in America/New_York), and on the fall-back date some times happen twice. The tool detects both by comparing the offset before and after the moment: for a gap it uses the instant just after the skip and shows a note, and for an ambiguous time it uses the earlier of the two occurrences and says so, rather than silently picking one.

faq.q: What is the year 2038 problem the tool mentions?
faq.a: Unix time stored in a signed 32-bit integer can only reach 2147483647, which is 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z. One second later the value overflows to a negative number, so systems using 32-bit time break. When you enter 2147483647 as seconds the tool shows this date and flags it. Modern 64-bit systems are not affected, but legacy code and some embedded devices still are.
